trips.title: Grandvalira & Pal-Arinsal: Andorra's Six-Sector Week
trips.summary: Andorra sells itself on volume, and for once the claim survives contact: Grandvalira alone strings six sectors across two valleys and a border ridge, and the joint Grandvalira Resorts ticket bolts on Pal-Arinsal and Ordino-Arcalís on the far side of the country. The week is built as a west-to-east sweep, start soft on Encamp and Canillo, spend the middle days working the Soldeu-Grau Roig spine and the Avet World Cup pitch, cross to Pas de la Casa for the French-facing snow, then break out to Arcalís for the one genuinely serious freeride mountain in the principality. It suits confident intermediates and better, families who want a lot of blue mileage without repetition, and anyone who likes the idea of finishing a ski day in a duty-free thermal spa. What it does not suit is the skier chasing Alpine altitude: the top here is 2,640 m and the bottom stations sit at 1,550-1,710 m, so snowmaking, not elevation, is what holds the week together.

trips.title: Jahorina & Bjelašnica: Sarajevo's Olympic Mountains in Winter
trips.sub: Jahorina, Bjelašnica & Igman, the 1984 Olympic mountains above Sarajevo
trips.summary: Sarajevo is the only European capital with two Olympic ski mountains inside forty minutes of its trams, and the week works because you can move between them. Jahorina, which held the 1984 women's alpine events, is the bigger and better-lifted of the pair, a broad forested dome of long blue and red motorway with a good gondola and the largest floodlit night-ski operation in the region. Bjelašnica, which held the men's, is the harder, colder, wind-scoured mountain, its summit plateau rolling out into the shepherd villages of Umoljani and Lukomir above the Rakitnica canyon. The arc is Jahorina first for volume, Bjelašnica second for character, Sarajevo as the constant bolt-hole, and one non-ski day given over to the city's Olympic ruins. It suits confident intermediates who care more about atmosphere and value than vertical, and anyone who wants a European ski week for half the Alpine price.

trips.title: Parnassos & Arachova: Skiing Above the Oracle
trips.sub: Mount Parnassos, Arachova & Delphi, Central Greece
trips.summary: Parnassos is the strangest ski week in Europe, and the reason to do it is not the skiing. It is the fact that you can spend a morning on a lift-served bowl at 2,200 m looking south over the Gulf of Corinth, and an afternoon walking the Sacred Way at **Delphi**, ten kilometres down the mountain, where the Greeks located the centre of the world. **Arachova**, a vertical stone village at 950 m clinging to the mountainside between the two, has spent thirty years turning itself into Greece's winter social capital, the ratio of fur coats to ski boots in its bars on a Saturday night is genuinely remarkable. The ski centre itself is state-run, with two linked sectors, **Kelaria** and **Fterolakka**, a third at **Gerontovrachos**, and Greece's first and only gondola lifts. The honest framing is this: the mountain is small, the season is short, the snow is unreliable, and you must build the week so that a bad snow report does not ruin it. This itinerary therefore alternates ski days with Delphi, the Corycian Cave, the north-side villages of **Agoriani/Eptalofos** and **Polydrosos**, and the tsipouro-and-formaela circuit, so that skiing is the bonus, not the premise.

trips.title: Sellaronda Week: Alta Badia & Val Gardena on One Pass
trips.sub: Alta Badia & Val Gardena, Dolomites, South Tyrol
trips.summary: This is the week the Dolomites were built for: one keycard, twelve ski areas, and a ring road on snow around a 3,152 m limestone block. The structure is simple, bed down in Alta Badia, spend the first days learning the local network at Corvara, La Villa and San Cassiano, run the **Sellaronda** once in each direction mid-week, take a day off the circuit for the **Hidden Valley** behind Lagazuoi, and cross into **Val Gardena** for the Saslong and Seceda. The skiing is overwhelmingly blue and red, immaculately groomed and rarely steep; what makes it remarkable is the scale, the light on the Sella and Sassolungo, and a rifugio culture in which lunch is a two-hour Ladin meal rather than a tray of chips. It suits confident intermediates above all, families who want distance without difficulty, and experts who accept that their hard skiing here is two World Cup pistes and a handful of couloirs rather than a whole mountain.

trips.title: Kopaonik: Pančićev Vrh, the Karaman Ridge and a Week on Serbia's Roof
trips.sub: Kopaonik National Park & Raška, southern Serbia
trips.summary: Kopaonik is the mountain Serbia built its winter around, and it is odd and likeable in ways the brochures do not capture: a broad, rounded massif rising to **Pančićev vrh at 2,017 m**, treeless on top, sun-drenched to a degree that has given it the nickname *Sunčana planina*, and equipped with an unusually good modern lift fleet including heated six-seaters and, since the Brzeće gondola opened, a genuine 1,000-metre vertical descent. The week is built as an inside-out exploration, two days learning the Suvo Rudište core around **Karaman Greben**, **Malo Jezero** and **Krst**, then out to the flanks at **Gobelja** and **Duboka**, then the full ride down the gondola to **Brzeće** and back, with the summit of Pančićev vrh saved for a clear morning. Kopaonik sits inside a national park, so the terrain is protected forest and open alpine meadow rather than a building site, and the après scene at Konaci is loud, cheap and entirely unlike anything in the Alps. It suits intermediates who want a lot of well-groomed red mileage, families who want night skiing and short lift lines mid-week, and travellers who like the idea of finishing the week in a 78°C thermal spring and a twelfth-century UNESCO monastery.

trips.summary: Chopok is a bald 2,024 m dome with a resort hanging off each side of it, and the whole week turns on which way the wind is blowing. North into Demänovská dolina you get glacial cirques, the Funitel, and free-ride…

trips.title: Kranjska Gora, Vogel & Krvavec: A Julian Alps Ski Week
trips.sub: Julian Alps & Gorenjska, Kranjska Gora, Planica, Bohinj and the Kamnik-Savinja fringe
trips.summary: Slovenia's ski week is not about one big mountain, there isn't one, but about four genuinely different ones inside an hour of each other, tied together by a hire car and a €16 vignette. **Kranjska Gora** is the World Cup village, low and tree-lined under the Vitranc ridge, with the **Podkoren** slalom and giant slalom courses on its doorstep and the **Planica** ski-flying hill five minutes up the valley. **Vogel**, reached by cable car from the shore of **Lake Bohinj**, is the opposite: a high shelf above a lake, with the best views and the most serious off-piste in the country. **Krvavec** sits eight kilometres from Ljubljana airport and delivers the highest, most reliable snow of the four. **Cerkno**, over the ridge in the Idrija hills, is the local's alternative when the Julian Alps are in cloud. The arc of the week runs Kranjska Gora first for the racing history and the easy legs, Vogel in the middle for the drama, Krvavec for altitude, and a full day on the **Pokljuka** biathlon plateau on snowshoes or skinny skis when the alpine legs need a break. It suits intermediates who would rather see four mountains than lap one, and anyone who values a €14 dinner and a thermal pool at the end of the day over lift-served vertical.

trips.title: Baqueira Beret: Val d'Aran on the Atlantic Side
trips.summary: Val d'Aran is the only Spanish valley that drains north into the Atlantic, and that single geographic accident is the whole trip: the weather arrives wet off the Bay of Biscay, dumps on the Aran side of the watershed, and leaves Baqueira with the most reliable snow in Spain. The week works as three concentric rings, the groomed Baqueira and Beret bowls for the first days, the Bonaigua and Cara Nord flanks for the harder pistes and long descents, and then the off-piste terrain around Baciver and the Escornacrabes couloir for anyone who brought a transceiver. Between ski days you drop into a valley of Romanesque churches, Aranese-speaking villages and thermal water at Tredòs. It suits strong intermediates and experts, especially those who care more about snow quality and freeride potential than about vertical drop or lift-network glamour.
